narrative:
The model predicts you have a 42% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to help you graduate.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this prediction were your lack of desire to pursue higher education, your clean record of zero past failures, and your relatively long daily commute to school. Surprisingly, not wanting to continue studying after high school was by far the strongest influence, pushing the model heavily toward expecting you to fail. Your zero past class failures worked in the opposite direction, pulling the prediction toward passing because students with no previous failures usually succeed. Your 30-to-60-minute travel time also nudged the outcome slightly toward passing, since most students who pass live much closer to school and spend less time commuting.

Because the negative effect of not planning for higher education was much larger than the positive effects of your clean record and commute, the model ultimately concluded you are at serious risk. To improve, you should seriously reflect on why you no longer want to continue your education and whether that goal can change. Even small shifts in motivation, combined with protecting your good record of no failures and reducing time lost to travel, could meaningfully raise your chances of passing. Taking the remedial courses seriously is a good first step toward turning this prediction around.
